The Story of the Five Hundred Monks

I bow to the feet of Lord Jinendra and I write the story of what happened to five hundred monks at once, which is the cause of welfare.

In the ancient city of the potter Katanam, south of Bharat's land, there ruled King Dandak, whose queen was Suvrata. Suvrata was beautiful and learned. The royal minister was named Balak. This sinner harboured great hatred for Jain dharma. One day, a group of five hundred monks came to the city. Minister Balak was very proud of his own scholarship. He went to the monks' Acharya for a scriptural debate. On the way, he met a monk named Khandak and immediately began arguing with him, speaking all manner of nonsense. The monk refuted his arguments so thoroughly, presenting the doctrine of Syadvad in such a masterful way, that Balak was silenced. He could not say another word. Defeated, he had to return home in shame. The fire of this humiliation burned fiercely in his heart. He resolved to take revenge.

For this purpose, he devised a scheme: he disguised a jester as a monk and sent him to Queen Suvrata's palace. This fake monk went to the queen and began making inappropriate jokes and playful remarks. Meanwhile, Balak told the king all about it, saying, "Maharaj, you show such devotion to these monks, always serving them — is this all for this day? Open your eyes and see what is happening right before you!" Seeing the jester's antics, the foolish King Dandak's fury knew no bounds. Blinded by anger, he immediately ordered, "Crush all the monks currently in my city in the oil press!"

The sinful minister had been waiting for just this. As soon as the royal order came, he did not waste a moment and immediately arranged for the monks to be crushed. In an instant, all five hundred monks were pressed in the oil press. Taking his revenge, Balak's soul was satisfied. Truly, those who are sinful, destined to suffer in lower births — those false-faith people do not hesitate to commit the most terrible sins, even if they must suffer for it birth after birth.

A terrible and unbearable atrocity was committed against the monastic community. But those brave, blessed monks did not utter a single complaint. They endured everything with perfect equanimity. Some of them, through the purity of their mental states, attained liberation right there. Others went to heaven. Through their silent strength and forbearance, they demonstrated the supreme power of spiritual practice.

The king and minister, having committed such a grave sin, suffered terribly. After death, they fell into the lowest hell, where they endured unimaginable suffering for countless ages. Eventually, through the ripening of residual merit, they regained human form and, through the grace of Jain dharma, found the path to liberation.

This story teaches that the forbearance of saints is their greatest strength. The five hundred monks, though innocent, endured the most terrible cruelty without anger or resentment. Their silent strength ultimately led to their liberation and the eventual redemption of their persecutors. The wise should cultivate forbearance and never resort to violence, even in the face of provocation.
